explanations.explanation: Water it is, friend. The LORD tells Jeremiah, the prophet, to put the loincloth around his waist, “…but do not let it touch water.” (Jeremiah 13:1) Linen that never gets a wash. I can't keep flour off my apron for ten minutes, so I'm impressed.

Fire makes sense in my line of work, but it's not in this verse. The LORD tells Jeremiah, the prophet, “…do not let it touch water.” (Jeremiah 13:1) The oven is my department. This loincloth just has to stay dry.

Oil isn't mentioned anywhere in this command. The LORD tells Jeremiah, the prophet, to wear the loincloth but “…do not let it touch water.” (Jeremiah 13:1) So the rule is about keeping it dry. Water is the word to hold onto.

True. Jeremiah says, “So I bought a loincloth in accordance with the word of the LORD, and I put it around my waist.” (Jeremiah 13:2) No arguing, no asking for a second opinion. I think a lot of us would have at least raised an eyebrow, and I have a LOT of eyebrow.

It's actually true. Jeremiah, the prophet, says he bought the loincloth "in accordance with the word of the LORD" and put it around his waist. (Jeremiah 13:2) He did exactly what he was told. Strange order, simple obedience.
The rocks, yes. The LORD says to hide the loincloth “…in a crevice of the rocks.” (Jeremiah 13:4) A crack in the rocks at Perath. Not a drawer, and believe me, I know the difference.

No temple in this verse, friend. The LORD tells Jeremiah, the prophet, to hide the loincloth at Perath “…in a crevice of the rocks.” (Jeremiah 13:4) The hiding spot is a crack in the rocks. Nothing fancy about it.

A wall sounds reasonable, but that's not what the text says. The LORD says to hide the loincloth at Perath “…in a crevice of the rocks.” (Jeremiah 13:4) So it's a crack in the rocks, not a wall. Jeremiah hides it there just as he was told. (Jeremiah 13:5)

explanations.answer: Ruined and of no use at all
explanations.explanation: Ruined, and that's the whole point. Jeremiah, the prophet, digs it up and finds that “…it was ruined…” (Jeremiah 13:7) It's of no use at all. After many days in the rocks, that loincloth was done. Now we get to hear why the LORD wanted it buried.

explanations.answer: Clean as the day he bought it
explanations.explanation: Not this time, friend. Jeremiah, the prophet, digs up the loincloth and finds it “…ruined…” and of no use at all. (Jeremiah 13:7) That is a long way from clean. It sat in the rocks for many days, and it showed.

explanations.answer: Faded but still fine to wear
explanations.explanation: Faded would be a gentle ending, but the text is harsher. Jeremiah, the prophet, digs it up and finds “…it was ruined…” and of no use at all. (Jeremiah 13:7) Nobody's wearing this one again. That's the picture the LORD wants him to see.

explanations.answer: The pride of Judah and Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: The pride, that's it. The LORD says, “…I will ruin the pride of Judah and the great pride of Jerusalem.” (Jeremiah 13:9) Judah is the southern kingdom, and Jerusalem is its capital. The ruined loincloth was a picture of that.

explanations.answer: The harvest of Judah and Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: The harvest isn't what the LORD names here. He says, “…I will ruin the pride of Judah and the great pride of Jerusalem.” (Jeremiah 13:9) Judah is the southern kingdom, and Jerusalem is its capital. The thing being ruined is their pride.

explanations.answer: The walls of Judah and Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Walls aren't mentioned in this verse. The LORD says, “…I will ruin the pride of Judah and the great pride of Jerusalem.” (Jeremiah 13:9) Judah is the southern kingdom, and Jerusalem is its capital. The word to catch is pride.

Gods, yes. The LORD says these people “…go after other gods to serve and worship them…” (Jeremiah 13:10) They refuse to listen to His words and follow their own stubborn hearts, too. That's a lot of ways to walk away from Him.
Nations don't appear in this verse. The LORD says these people “…go after other gods to serve and worship them…” (Jeremiah 13:10) You serve and worship gods, not nations. That's the word that fits.

Kings do show up later in the passage, but not here. In this verse the LORD says these people “…go after other gods to serve and worship them…” (Jeremiah 13:10) The problem is who they were serving and worshiping. Other gods.

explanations.answer: To be His people for His glory
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the LORD gives. He made them cling to Him “…so that they might be My people for My renown and praise and glory.” (Jeremiah 13:11) A loincloth stays close to the waist, and He wanted them close to Him. Then the verse says it plainly: “But they did not listen.”

explanations.answer: To keep them safe from every war
explanations.explanation: Safe from every war isn't the reason in this verse. The LORD says He made them cling to Him “…so that they might be My people for My renown and praise and glory.” (Jeremiah 13:11) The text gives that reason and no other. I'd rather bake what the verse says than add my own.

explanations.answer: To make them richer than the nations
explanations.explanation: Riches aren't mentioned here. The LORD says He made them cling to Him “…so that they might be My people for My renown and praise and glory.” (Jeremiah 13:11) The reason is that they would be His people. That's the answer in the verse.

The text says the opposite, friend. The LORD says He made them cling to Him, “But they did not listen.” (Jeremiah 13:11) That's the sad end of the verse. They stayed close, and then they stopped listening.

False, and the verse says so plainly. After the LORD says He made Israel and Judah cling to Him, He adds, “But they did not listen.” (Jeremiah 13:11) That one sentence is a heavy way to end the picture. The loincloth clung, and they didn't hear.

That's the reply. The people answer, “Don’t we surely know that every wineskin should be filled with wine?” (Jeremiah 13:12) Basically, "Jeremiah, tell us something we don't know." We've all given that look to somebody explaining the obvious.

explanations.answer: Then bring us the wine now
explanations.explanation: Nobody's calling for wine in this verse. The people reply, “Don’t we surely know that every wineskin should be filled with wine?” (Jeremiah 13:12) They're saying they already know it. No refills requested.

Empty wineskins don't come up here. The people reply, “Don’t we surely know that every wineskin should be filled with wine?” (Jeremiah 13:12) They're saying they know this already. It's the first time in this passage that the people speak.

Not true. The LORD says He will fill with drunkenness “…all who live in this land—the kings who sit on David’s throne, the priests, the prophets, and all the people of Jerusalem.” (Jeremiah 13:13) The kings and the priests are named right in the list. This is a heavy line, and nobody is left out of it.

False, and the verse names them. The LORD says He will fill with drunkenness “…all who live in this land—the kings who sit on David’s throne, the priests, the prophets, and all the people of Jerusalem.” (Jeremiah 13:13) David was Israel's king, and these kings sit on his throne. This part of the passage is heavy, and nobody is skipped.

It's the other way around, friend. The LORD says, “I will allow no mercy or pity or compassion to keep Me from destroying them.” (Jeremiah 13:14) Those three things won't hold Him back. This is the hardest line in the passage, and it's good to say that out loud.

False. The LORD says, “I will allow no mercy or pity or compassion to keep Me from destroying them.” (Jeremiah 13:14) None of those three will stop Him. I think this is a hard verse to sit with, and that's okay.
